analysis.one_liner: Requires states to let voters register and vote on the same day, including during early voting.
analysis.headline: The Same Day Registration Act was introduced in October 2009 with 4 Senate cosponsors, sent to the Senate Rules Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Help America Vote Act to require every state to let eligible voters register at the polling place on election day — and on early voting days — and cast a ballot right then. It was aimed at people who miss their state's registration deadline, typically younger and more mobile voters. It never advanced past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Eligible voters who miss their state's registration deadline — disproportionately young people, renters, and people who move often — could show up on election day or during early voting, register on the spot, and vote. States with no registration requirement are exempt.

how_it_helps.text: States must permit any eligible individual to register at the polling place and vote on election day and on any early voting day, overriding federal rules that set earlier registration deadlines.
The requirement would have applied starting with the November 2010 federal election and all elections after that.
States that have no voter registration requirement at all are exempt, leaving current same-day-friendly systems untouched.

analysis.who_pays: State and local election administrators would bear the cost of staffing polling places to verify identity and register voters on the spot, on the bill's timeline — it would have taken effect for the election barely a year after introduction.

drawbacks.text: Same-day registration shifts registration work from clerks' offices to the polling place, requiring more trained poll workers, verification equipment, and provisional-ballot safeguards on a compressed timeline; states would bear those administrative costs without new funding in the bill.
Requiring compliance for the November 2010 election, when the bill was introduced in late October 2009, gave states and localities very little lead time to retrain staff and update procedures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: same-day registration reliably raises turnout among voters most likely to be missed by deadlines, and a dozen states already run such systems. The cost is administrative — local election offices would need more workers and procedures — and the short runway to November 2010 made compliance harder than it needed to be. On balance it is a modest, workable voting-access change that costs states money and never received a debate or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Feingold introduced the bill on October 28, 2009, joined by Sens. Klobuchar, Tester, Harkin, and Kerry.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
No committee action, floor vote, or further step appears in the action history for the rest of the 111th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State election offices were spared new compliance costs, and the existing registration-deadline system — and the parties advantaged by it — remained unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State election offices and the registration status quo

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Same Day Registration Act and spoke for it on introduction.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Charles Schumer, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no Republican support appears in the record, but there were no votes, so the partisan shape of the full Senate was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed new same-day registration duties and costs on state and local election offices, with no funding attached. Voters in those states, however, would have gained a way to vote they currently lack.
